extracted.intended_audience: writers of historical fiction (beginners through experienced authors)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for authors crafting historical fiction novels and stories, focusing on balancing historical accuracy, research, characterization, language, and story integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish rules for when to bend history
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish your own set of rules for when to bend history for the sake of the story—and stick to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are many opinions on accuracy; rather than never deviating, make fair and consistent decisions. Distinguish between altering verifiable facts and filling in gaps: if something can't be verified you have more freedom. Back up interpretations via research. Changes should be plausible (e.g., don't move someone earlier if they were imprisoned then). Lesser-known figures allow more maneuvering, but invented material should be consistent with known traits (behaviour, interests, values). The author links to a free official guide to accuracy and authenticity for more tips.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do plenty of research but be selective in what you include
rubrics_metrics.description: Do plenty of research—but know what to include and what not to include in your novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with secondary sources and use primary sources (letters, newspapers, diaries). Visit archives and relevant historical sites where possible; read period fiction, cook period food, find recordings/recreations of music. Expect to discard roughly 95% of your research from the manuscript: the sum total of research should inform the world, but only small, carefully chosen details should appear on the page. Avoid dumping research; selective deployment immerses readers. Keep notes even if you don't use everything.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include non-conformist characters but provide context
rubrics_metrics.description: Include characters who break the conventions and norms of their period—but don't forget to include context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: History contains exceptions; depicting only conforming people removes variation and change. When portraying non-conformity, show it as exceptional—illustrate obstacles, conflict, ostracisation, and the consequences those characters face so readers accept their authenticity. Avoid presenting anachronistic behaviour as normal without demonstrating why it's exceptional in that era.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use readable language rather than historically literal speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't write like you're in the 14th century.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dialogue should give an impression of period authenticity while remaining readable. Avoid archaic, unintelligible language (e.g., Chaucerian speech) that will lose modern readers, and also avoid modern colloquialisms. Use mostly neutral language with a sprinkling of archaic words or constructions that are still recognizable. Temper older nineteenth-century language for modern readers as needed. The goal is a literary 'sleight of hand' that suggests historical distance without sacrificing readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate history organically into the story
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrate the history seamlessly into the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrate historical forces through scenes and character actions (e.g., Dickens' scene that embodies causes of the French Revolution) rather than summarising or large expository blocks. Avoid sending characters into situations solely to display research (banquets, armories) or dedicating long passages to historical context. Details must fit naturally around the plot; show rather than tell to keep reader engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritise perceived authenticity over awkward factual accuracy (use narrative workarounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't insist on accuracy if it will cause disbelief (but here's a workaround if you really must).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a true historical fact will seem ludicrous to modern readers and harm believability, consider omitting it—the impression of accuracy often matters more than strict factuality for reader acceptance. If you must include an unbelievable historical detail, incorporate characters' scepticism into the narrative and have another character validate the fact within the story; this reassures the reader and mitigates disbelief.
